Arize evaluates agent outputs and behaviour on the customer's production traces (spans, traces, sessions) and on datasets and experiments before release. Criteria are customer-written or built-in templates scored by LLM judges, code checks or human annotation, such as correctness, hallucination and agent trajectory quality.

  • Production quality scoring: online evals on spans, traces and sessions with LLM judges, code checks, agent-as-judge, Decision Judge or human review; example criteria are helpfulness, tone, correctness, hallucination and trajectory.
  • Pre-release experiments: offline evals on datasets and experiments, run in CI/CD, and prompt comparison in a playground before deploying.
  • LLM red teaming: adversarial prompt datasets for prompt injection, harmful content, data privacy and misinformation, scored before deployment (docs); cost per trace is tracked separately.

Judgment evaluates the traces of a customer's production agents with customer-defined judges, and groups recurring failures it discovers on its own. The same judges score agent runs on offline test suites of customer-built cases. Criteria are rubrics, conditions and code written by the customer.

  • Production quality scoring: agentic judges apply customer rubrics and labels to live traces and sessions; condition judges check duration, LLM cost and errors; custom code judges; judges can be aligned to human labels.
  • Issue discovery: a background agent reads recent traces and reports recurring failures by root cause, severity and evidence.
  • Offline test suites: cases with expected judge answers run on a dataset to gate pull requests and compare models or prompts.

Raindrop evaluates how production agents behave, using the customer's live traces and, in Simulations, replayed production traffic and test cases. It scores deviations from forecast normal for tool errors, latency and user signals, and judges whether a fix improves behaviour. Criteria are learned from traffic or defined by the team as Signals.

  • Production issue detection: anomaly detection on tool error rate, latency and signals, with severity from user impact; issues carry a confidence score; underlying model not published.

  • Simulations (early access): replays production traffic and existing test cases against a change on each pull request and applies anomaly detection to the results.

G2 tests vendors' live AI agents itself, in a simulated company with customers, order data, a written support policy and tools, and scores every agent on four criteria: accuracy, policy compliance, relevance and completeness. Tasks carry point values that sum to an Overall Score. The whole program is in beta, and vendors review results before publication but cannot change their score.

  • Policy compliance: an LLM judge checks whether the agent followed the written policy it was given; no regulation or standard is named.
  • Accuracy, relevance and completeness: LLM judges score claims against evidence and focus on the user's problem; completeness is deterministic and checks that required outcomes happened in the underlying systems.
  • Agent categories: customer experience, AI SDR, marketing, legal, recruiting, voice, security, accounting, coding and IT support agents; security is a product category, not a test type.

G2 refreshes evaluations several times a year. It is a beta program, and there is no certificate or insurance.

Seeding, reset and persistence are not documented, so a stateful twin is claimed only. The object is the full agent (model, retrieval, actions, guardrails, workflows). Beta.

It uses G2's written policy, not a customer's own. It ties to no regulation. Results are public in a ranked leaderboard (for example Retell 243 and Yuma 240 among customer-experience agents). Coded early because the program is in beta.

METR measures what frontier AI agents can do on long autonomous tasks and assesses whether developers could lose control of them. It scores task completion (time horizon at 50% and 80% success), runs red-team tests of agent monitors, and publishes the results; labs and government institutes use it.

Third Party: METR's outputs go to the people who deploy or oversee frontier models. It does frontier-agent risk assessments for AI labs, gives technical help to regulators (named: the UK AI Security Institute and the EU AI Office), and publishes time-horizon measurements and reports for the public and for third parties to read. The form is reports and published results with raw data, not a certificate or insurance product. METR is an independent nonprofit.

Simulation: METR runs AI agents on suites of long tasks (software, machine learning, cyber) and on loss-of-control risk evaluations, with success checked automatically. The environment is real sandboxed task environments with shell tools, not stubs, so it is coded as a real system. The objects are frontier models and the agents built on them. The pages do not describe a stateful twin of business systems or customer-policy testing.

Benchmark: The Time Horizon benchmark (version 1.1 on the page, with a dated change log, version 1.0 kept and raw data available) measures the length of tasks, in human time, that an agent completes at 50 percent and 80 percent success. A public multi-model comparison lists many frontier models. The page says it is no longer actively updated. It is a generalized measure and does not apply a customer's own policy, and no tie to a regulation or standard is stated.

2018 (first AI policy)		Mature
A unit of the listed reinsurer Munich Re, with about 43,982 staff in the group (December 2025); the unit's own size is not published.		Horizontal

1Evaluate: Insurer rule R5: reviews the model's data science process and tests the performance metric before cover (munichre.com insure-ai page; search of Emerj and Munich Re pages, ).

0Control: No in-path mechanism; insurance cover only.

🟡 Output quality❌ Cost and performance❌ Security❌ Behavior and compliance

Munich Re's data scientists review how the AI model is built and tested, then estimate from the provider's historical performance data how likely it is to underperform. The provider and Munich Re agree where the model is valid and which performance metric counts; the guarantee threshold comes from that metric's probability distribution, and the payout grows with the shortfall. The model's quality and stability set the premium, and the provider keeps part of the risk through coinsurance. Claims are settled on measured performance against the threshold, with the provider locking predictions and supplying ground truth.

  • Who evaluates: Munich Re's own data scientists and research team do the review, with domain experts added case by case, for example a cyber team for a malware model.
  • What is checked: data generation and annotation, training and testing procedure, retraining, drift risk and input and output statistics.
  • Method: the risk estimator uses conformal prediction on historical performance, and a 2023 paper co-authored by Munich Re's Michael Berger shows its failure probabilities to be conservative.
  • Terms effect: premium follows model quality and stability, the threshold follows the metric's distribution, and exclusions, deductibles and limits apply.
  • Trigger and limits: a parametric-like payout on a pre-agreed measurable threshold with no negligence needed; discrimination and fines are covered losses but no test for them was found, and malicious attacks are described as outside the performance product.
Audience Third Party

Evaluate mode none

Benchmark none

Third Party: aiSure is sold to two groups: AI vendors, who use it to back a performance warranty for their customers (for example a guaranteed model accuracy or ROI), and corporations deploying AI, who buy cover for losses from AI errors such as lost revenue, business interruption, legal damages and hallucination-related harm. The recipient of the output is the third party that relies on the model: a vendor's client holding an insured warranty, or the deployer holding a policy. They receive a policy or warranty backing that pays out on eligible losses; a LiveEO TradeAware case on EUDR compliance is the named example. Whether any score, report or certificate accompanies the policy is not documented.

Insurance: This is Insurance, coded as shipping. Munich Re, a reinsurer and carrier, writes the performance guarantee and the cover for AI errors. Before writing cover, Munich Re says it reviews the model's data science process and tests the performance metric (an underwriting review; the source is the product page and a press interview, not a published standard). The scope covers vendor warranties, AI liabilities (discrimination, IP infringement, hallucinations, regulatory fines) and own financial loss for deployers. Assurance is not set, and no accreditation or named test standard is documented.

AIUC certifies AI agents against its own AIUC-1 standard: six domains (data and privacy, security, safety, reliability, accountability, society) with about 50 live requirements. Accredited auditors review controls; AIUC itself runs the technical evals, typically 1,000 to 5,000 scenarios, quarterly. The certificate lasts 12 months and carries an audit report.

  • Conduct requirements: safety (C003 harmful outputs, C004 out-of-scope outputs, C007 human review of high-risk outputs), reliability (D001 hallucination, D003 unsafe tool calls) and accountability; test suites are not published.
  • Evals and report: AIUC runs the evals on the agent before certification and retests quarterly; the audit report holds the results. A sample of 85,000 graded evaluations found issues in 22.0% of ordinary requests against 2.9% of adversarial attacks.
  • Crosswalks: AIUC-1 is mapped to the EU AI Act (by article), ISO/IEC 42001 (by clause), NIST AI RMF, SOC 2, NYC Local Law 144 and the Colorado AI Act; the mapping is content, and AIUC claims no presumed conformity.

  • AI TAP: technical, operational and financial evaluation of testers; first accredited are AIDX Tech, Knovel Engineering, PwC Singapore, Resaro and Vulcan (press); Resaro also helped shape the kit.

Third Party: The foundation's toolkits are for application developers, deployers, enterprises and accredited testers who test LLM apps they deploy; no buyer or procurement use is shown. Third-party readers are the governments and assessors served by its resources: IMDA's Starter Kits for safety testing of LLM apps and of agentic systems, the Model Governance Framework for agentic AI, Sandbox case studies, and the AI Tester Accreditation programme, which accredits testers, not systems. AI Verify produces test reports and process checks that a company can show to others, but there is no certificate about an AI system.

Simulation: Project Moonshot is an open-source toolkit that runs benchmark tests and red teaming against LLMs and LLM applications. The environment is prompt-level: datasets and attack prompts are sent to a model or app endpoint and scored with evaluators tuned to the benchmark datasets recommended in IMDA's Starter Kit. No mocked tools, stateful twin or real-system run is documented. The objects are models and LLM applications. IMDA has also published a Starter Kit for testing agentic systems, but no agent-testing product detail was found.

Benchmark: Moonshot implements the benchmarks recommended in IMDA's Starter Kit for Safety Testing of LLM-based Applications and can be used out of the box. The page names no specific versioned dataset, so the benchmark flag is claimed. The testing methodology is tied to IMDA's recommendations, and AI Verify process checks (mapped to ISO/IEC 42001 and NIST AI RMF) complement it. There is no custom judge applying a customer's own policy and no public leaderboard.

🟡 Output quality❌ Cost and performance✅ Security❌ Behavior and compliance

RiskRubric is CSA's rating system that scores AI models, MCP servers and AI agents from 0 to 100 and A to F. V2 replaces the Reputation pillar with Excessive Agency and adds a confidence index based on the number of independent scanners. Scanners by Deloitte Italy, PointGuard and Tumeryk run the tests under CSA's methodology.

  • Six pillars: Transparency, Reliability, Security, Privacy, Safety and Excessive Agency, weighted 16, 16, 20, 16, 16 and 16 percent; the original engine combined automated red-teaming with open-source intelligence.
  • Agent and MCP assessment: agents evaluated on end-to-end task execution; MCP servers on tool-surface integrity, tool-call abuse resistance and supply-chain risk.
  • Scanner rules: scanners must retain raw test artifacts, declare methodology version and disclose affiliation; criteria are CSA's own, not a regulation.

Buyer and Third Party: RiskRubric is CSA's public rating of AI models. Each rated service gets a 0-100 score and an A-F grade with supporting indicators across pillars. Buyers can use the grades in procurement and deployment decisions, such as choosing a model, and developers check the scorecards before choosing. Third parties with no relationship to the rated vendor can read the scores, which are published rather than issued as a certificate.

Simulation: RiskRubric scans each model with an evaluation engine that combines automated red teaming with open-source intelligence collection. The environment is prompt-level, with adversarial and benign prompts sent to model endpoints. The tested object is the model. V2 plans to add agents (scored on end-to-end task execution) and MCP servers through federated scanners, but this was announced for a Q3 2026 launch and no post-launch evidence was found, so agent coverage is only claimed.

Benchmark: RiskRubric is a named, versioned scoring methodology: V1 launched in September 2025 with six pillars (Transparency, Reliability, Security, Privacy, Safety, Reputation), and V2 (concept paper, 2026) replaces Reputation with Excessive Agency and reweights the pillars. Scanners must retain raw artifacts, declare the methodology version and disclose affiliation. Scores appear on a public leaderboard at riskrubric.ai, as reported by the press (the site could not be opened). It is a generalized benchmark with no custom judge function and no stated tie to a specific regulation.
